---
title: "Missing data"
---

Suppose a vowel production study records duration and three formants for every token. The third formant tracker fails on some tokens, so the corresponding cells are blank. The blanks create a software problem because many functions expect a rectangular table. But filling or deleting the cells merely to satisfy the software would begin at the wrong place. As in the earlier discussion of [exclusion rules](../experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd), the process determining which observations enter an analysis can change the quantity being estimated.

Each blank records a measurement that could have been present but is absent. The reason for that absence may affect what an analysis estimates. A tracker that fails at random removes a different set of tokens from a tracker that fails on unusually high formant values. The visible table may not tell these cases apart.

The process that removes values determines which claims the retained data can support. An analysis thus requires two objects. The first is the linguistic measurement that might be absent. The second is an indicator recording whether that measurement was observed. Keeping the two objects separate prevents a blank from being treated as though it were a measured value.

## Three questions precede imputation

[**Imputation**](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-historic.html) replaces a missing value with one or more estimates. The replacement is produced by a model or rule. It is not a newly observed measurement.

Before choosing a procedure, ask three questions.

1. Which measurements are absent, and where do their absences occur?
2. What process could have made those measurements absent?
3. Which population or relation would an analysis of the observed subset estimate?

The first question concerns an observed pattern. The second concerns a data-generating process, some parts of which may be unobserved. The third concerns the estimand. These questions are connected, but they are not interchangeable. A visible association between vowel category and tracker failure does not prove why the tracker failed, and a plausible account of failure does not show how many rows an analysis will lose.

## How the module proceeds

We begin with [missingness patterns](missingness-patterns.qmd). That page defines a missingness indicator and uses it to count absent values by row, column, and pattern. [Missingness mechanisms](missingness-mechanisms.qmd) then distinguishes three claims about how that indicator depends on observed and unobserved measurements.

[Complete case analysis](complete-case-analysis.qmd) studies the consequences of deleting any row with a missing analysis variable. This procedure is simple, but the retained rows may represent a selected population and can be far fewer than the missing percentage for any one column suggests.

Only then do we turn to [iterative PCA imputation](pca-imputation.qmd). This page depends on the earlier factorization sequence because the imputation repeatedly centers a matrix, fits a low rank representation, and reconstructs missing cells. The statistical object introduced here is the imputation iteration, not principal component analysis itself.

Finally, [validating an imputation procedure](validating-imputation.qmd) hides observed values and checks whether the procedure reconstructs them without access to their true values during fitting. This validation cannot reveal the naturally missing values, but it can show where an imputation procedure fails on observed values made artificially unavailable.

## What the module does not assume

No generic procedure makes missing data harmless. Complete case analysis may be adequate under a narrow selection claim. A low rank imputation may work when several measurements share stable linear structure. Neither procedure can establish its own assumptions from the completed table.

This limitation is useful. It forces the report to distinguish what was observed, what was assumed about absence, what was estimated from the retained or completed data, and what remains uncertain because the missing values were never measured.

## What this module adds

By the end of the module, we should be able to encode missingness separately from a linguistic response, state what each missingness mechanism claims, determine how deletion changes the analysis set, and evaluate an imputation on values that were hidden on purpose. We begin by making the pattern of blank cells explicit.
